Xylanase is widely used in broiler nutrition to degrade fiber and improve nutrient availability across diet types. It also reduces digesta viscosity in diets containing wheat or other viscous cereals.³˒⁴˒⁵ Solutions such as[Danisco® Xylanase](https://www.iff.com/animal-nutrition/products/danisco-xylanase/) are applied in cereal-based diets rich in non-starch polysaccharides (NSPs), where these functions remain highly relevant.


Those functions remain essential, but nutritionists now face a broader challenge: supporting early gut robustness, immune resilience, and consistent performance, particularly in antibiotic-free systems and amid increasing raw-material variability.


Cereal quality varies according to where and how crops are grown, while differences in NSP composition can affect nutrient availability and gut dynamics. These variations are especially consequential during the starter phase, when digestive capacity is still developing.[Animal nutrition](https://www.iff.com/animal-nutrition/) specialists therefore need strategies that support early gut development while delivering more consistent results from variable feed ingredients.


In this context, Danisco® Xylanase enzyme is increasingly being recognized not only as an efficiency enzyme but also as a targeted gut health strategy, especially at higher inclusion levels. New data show that high-dose xylanase supplementation not only improves digestibility but also influences the gut microbiome during early life, enhances intestinal integrity, and translates these biological advantages into clear, measurable performance gains.

## Arabinoxylans in Poultry Diets: From Antinutritional Factor to Functional Opportunity


Corn and wheat are principal ingredients in broiler diets worldwide. They also contain high levels of arabinoxylans, the main non-starch polysaccharides in cereal cell walls.⁶˒⁷ These arabinoxylan-rich structures can encapsulate starch and protein, restricting access by endogenous enzymes—particularly in young birds, whose digestive capacity is still developing.⁵


The effects of arabinoxylans depend on their structure and solubility. Soluble fractions can increase digesta viscosity, while insoluble fractions contribute to the physical encapsulation of nutrients. Together, these effects can limit nutrient utilization unless the arabinoxylans are effectively degraded.¹


Arabinoxylans have traditionally been viewed as antinutritional components to be neutralized. However, this perspective overlooks their potential value. When effectively broken down, they release functional oligosaccharides that beneficial gut bacteria can ferment.


The opportunity, then, lies in unlocking this fiber efficiently so that it can support gut health and performance.


## How Danisco® Xylanase Enzyme Supports Poultry Gut Health Beyond Digestibility


Danisco® Xylanase is[designed](https://www.iff.com/our-science/) to act at the optimal pH and location in the gastrointestinal tract, enabling efficient arabinoxylan degradation in cereal-based diets.


In the upper gut, this results in well-established benefits:


- Cleavage of arabinoxylans
- Reduced digesta viscosity in diets containing wheat or other viscous cereals
- Improved nutrient release
- Increased nutrient absorption at the site of uptake


However, its effects are not limited to the upper gut. Early hydrolysis of arabinoxylans not only improves immediate nutrient access but also influences the type and quantity of fiber fragments that reach the lower gut.


Danisco® Xylanase enzyme breaks down arabinoxylans found in cereals to generate small fiber fragments called arabinoxylo-oligosaccharides (AXOS). These AXOS:


- Resist host digestion
- Reach the lower gut intact
- Serve as substrates for beneficial bacteria


By generating AXOS, Danisco® Xylanase enzyme helps shape the substrates available to microorganisms in the hindgut. This contributes to a prebiotic-like effect that supports microbial fermentation and gut function alongside feed efficiency, linking enzyme activity in the upper gastrointestinal tract to microbial responses farther along the digestive system.


## Why Xylanase Inclusion Level Influences Outcomes in Broilers


Xylanase inclusion level plays an important role in determining functional outcomes in broilers. At lower inclusion levels, the primary effect is typically arabinoxylan cleavage and improved nutrient release. At higher inclusion levels, more extensive arabinoxylan hydrolysis may generate more AXOS and exert a stronger influence on microbial activity in the lower gut.²˒⁸


This represents a shift from effects driven mainly by digestibility toward a combination of digestive and microbiome responses. It is especially relevant in young broilers, where increased digestive capacity and early microbial colonization can together influence long-term performance.


## AXOS Profile and Microbial Cross-Feeding: Why Enzyme Specificity Matters


The functional effects of xylanase enzyme depend on the types and size distribution of the oligosaccharides produced. Danisco® Xylanase generates a spectrum of AXOS, including:


- **Short-chain AXOS and XOS** : Rapidly fermented by primary bacterial fermenters, producing acetate and lactate
- **Longer-chain AXOS** : Fermented more slowly, reaching the ceca, where they support butyrate-producing bacteria


This balance drives microbial cross-feeding, in which metabolites produced by one bacterial group are utilized by others, resulting in a sustained increase in butyrate production and improvement in gut barrier integrity.⁹


In practical terms, the result is a more stable and sustained fermentation pattern rather than short-lived fluctuations. This is particularly relevant during early gut development, when microbial populations are still becoming established.


*Proposed microbial cross-feeding pathway following xylanase enzyme-mediated breakdown of cereal arabinoxylans. Xylo-oligomers (DP2–9) are fermented by primary fermenters to produce lactate and acetate, which are then utilized by secondary, butyrate-producing bacteria. The resulting butyrate supports epithelial barrier function and immune development.*

## What Happens in the Gut: Measurable, Sequential Improvements


In a controlled broiler starter study (days 1–11) using a mixed-grain diet, Danisco® Xylanase enzyme inclusion increased beneficial bacteria linked to short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production:


- ***Bifidobacterium*** prevalence increased by up to 12.1%
- ***Butyricicoccus*** prevalence increased by up to 43.8%
- ***Blautia*** relative abundance increased by up to 45.2%


*Danisco® Xylanase enzyme at 8,000 U/kg increased the relative abundance of Blautia by 45.2% during early life (days 1–11) compared with a control diet.*


The observed increase in this bacterial population reflects a functional shift toward a butyrate-producing microbiome. Alongside these microbiome changes, several markers associated with gut barrier function showed increased expression:


- ***Toll-like receptor 4*** (TLR-4) expression increased by 166%
- ***Claudin-1*** (CLDN-1) tight junction expression increased by 229%
- ***Zonula occludens-1*** (ZO-1) tight junction expression increased by 211%


*Danisco® Xylanase enzyme at 8,000 U/kg increased gene expression of toll-like receptor 4 (TLR-4), claudin-1 (CLDN-1), and zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) during early life in broilers compared with a control diet. Values that do not share a superscript letter differ significantly (p < 0.05).*


Together, these responses are consistent with a more structured gut barrier and modified microbial activity. The associated changes in gut signaling and barrier function affect how the gut interacts with luminal contents. In turn, these changes can support nutrient utilization and create an environment better suited to performance, feed efficiency, and early-life robustness.


A stronger gut barrier can reduce intestinal permeability and immune activation costs, supporting more efficient nutrient utilization and allowing more energy to be directed toward growth.


## Linking Gut Function to Performance Outcomes


The biological responses observed with Danisco® Xylanase enzyme at higher inclusion levels were accompanied by measurable performance outcomes.


**Higher bodyweight** : Bodyweight increased by 7.7% at day 11 and 2.9% at day 42 compared with the control.


*Danisco® Xylanase enzyme at 8,000 U/kg increased broiler bodyweight by 7.7% at day 11 and 2.9% at day 42 compared with a control diet. Values that do not share a superscript letter differ significantly (p < 0.05).*


**Improved feed conversion ratio:** FCR improved by 8 points at day 11 and 7 points at day 42 compared with the control.


*Danisco® Xylanase enzyme at 8,000 U/kg reduced FCR by 8 points (6.7%) during days 1–11 and 7 points (4.3%) during days 1–42 compared with a control diet. Values that do not share a superscript letter differ significantly (p < 0.05).*


These improvements are particularly relevant in the starter phase, where inefficiencies are difficult to recover later in the production cycle. Even incremental gains at this stage can influence flock uniformity and final performance outcomes.


This alignment between digestive efficiency, microbiome modulation, and gut integrity markers indicates that Danisco® Xylanase contributes to performance through multiple, complementary mechanisms.


## Implications for Broiler Nutrition Strategies


For nutritionists, these findings support a broader view of Danisco® Xylanase enzyme, not only as a tool for nutrient release but also as part of a gut functionality strategy.


This broader role is particularly relevant in:


- Antibiotic-free production systems
- Diets with variable fiber composition
- Situations requiring improved early gut development and robustness


## Rethinking the Role of Xylanase Enzyme in Broiler Nutrition


Xylanase remains a key enzyme for improving feed efficiency. At higher inclusion levels, Danisco® Xylanase enzyme extends this traditional role by supporting microbial activity, fiber utilization, and gut function.


For nutritionists, this broader functionality can mean more gain from the same feed, greater robustness during the high-risk early phase, and more predictable performance later in the production cycle. These outcomes are increasingly important as production systems face growing demands for consistency and resilience.


Taken together, these findings support viewing xylanase enzyme not as a single-purpose enzyme focused mainly on nutrient release but as a[multifunctional contributor](https://www.iff.com/media/stories/optimizing-phytase-animal-feed/) to gut health and performance.
